item.title: Combining Multiple Incomplete Astronomical Surveys to Estimate Galaxy Flux Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2610.37855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In astrophysics, the distributions of fluxes or intensities of populations of sources provide insight into the structure and evolution of the universe. We propose a science-driven hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the X-ray flux distribution of a population of galaxies. The distribution is parameterized via a broken power law model, formulated as a mixture of Pareto distributions, and is fit using data from a combination of non-representative X-ray and optical surveys. Because fainter sources are less likely to be detected, astronomical surveys suffer from incompleteness at the low-intensity end, and dedicated survey simulations are used to study the resulting missing-data pattern and determine the form of corrections. We introduce a methodology to combine data from two (or more) surveys with different incompleteness functions. This allows us to leverage deeper surveys (e.g., optical) to more fully characterize the X-ray log(N)-log(S) (where fewer sources are detected). We take advantage of a well-calibrated characterization of the missing-data pattern, particularly in X-ray surveys, to make incompleteness corrections for sources that are not detected in either survey. The proposed model is validated using a simulation study designed to mimic the Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S), demonstrating accurate recovery of the flux distribution even under high proportions of systematic incompleteness. Finally, we apply our proposed method to data from the CDF-S.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Autenrieth, David A. van Dyk, Vinay Kashyap, Andreas Zezas, Aneta Siemiginowska, David C. Stenning

item.title: Opening Rankings from Engine Self-Play Are Less Certain Than They Look: Sampling Error, Draws, and Strength Dependence in Strength-Limited Stockfish Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.37988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Engine self-play allows chess openings to be compared under controlled conditions, without the selection effects of human game databases. When openings differ only slightly, however, rankings built from a few hundred games can be unstable. In Study 1, strength-limited Stockfish 15.1 played 17,400 games: ten forced White first moves and ten forced Black replies to 1.e4, each at three strength settings. The leading opening changed between settings, twice by a single game. There was no statistically reliable evidence, though, that differences among openings depended on strength (White p = .311, Black p = .843). The design had limited sensitivity to isolated strength-dependent effects: a 12-point effect was detected by the omnibus test in only about 39% of simulated studies. A Connect Four positive control detected an observed 22.5-point center-column advantage, demonstrating sensitivity to large opening differences. With 290 games per opening, the observed leader was the true best of ten openings in only about 44% of simulated studies assuming a between-opening standard deviation of three percentage points. Follow-up studies with complete game records showed that the settings were ordered in direct matches but did not form a consistent Elo scale, that win and draw rates differed across hardware and implementation configurations, and that an apparent 1.d3 weakness was not confirmed in new games. With Stockfish 19 and a fixed node budget, survey-selected replies showed no statistically reliable advantage over free engine choice. Opening leaderboards from a few hundred engine games can overstate certainty.
item.dc:creator: Conrad Flick, Jaysen Jensen, Jingyu Huang, Mario Camara Paslar

item.title: A simple sensitivity analysis for observational studies
item.description: arXiv:2610.38270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Drawing causal conclusions from non-experimental (observational) data is a central aim in science but is extremely challenging. Without control over treatment assignment (as in an experiment), treated and control groups may not be comparable on unmeasured factors affecting treatment and outcome. To address such concerns, sensitivity analyses can be performed; sensitivity analyses acknowledge the existence of unmeasured factors but ask how strong they must be to overturn causal conclusions. We (re)introduce a particularly simple form of sensitivity analysis which can be performed by any reader of an observational study with access to only an estimate and confidence interval for a causal effect. This simple sensitivity analysis may serve as an effective tool for readers wishing to gauge the robustness of conclusions from an observational study.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Zhang, Dylan S. Small

item.title: Length-Preserving Vessel Trajectory Simplification With Controllable Compression-Precision Bound
item.description: arXiv:2610.38295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vessel trajectory data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS) is important for a wide range of maritime analysis and management applications. As AIS datasets continue to grow in scale, trajectory simplification (or compression) algorithms have become indispensable tools for managing their computational demands. Existing approaches, however, largely overlook the preservation of trajectory length, a critical metric of direct relevance to maritime environmental auditing and voyage management. We address this gap by framing trajectory simplification as a pair of dual optimization problems subject to error constraints: Compression-Driven Simplification (CDS), which minimizes data volume for a given length-error tolerance, and Precision-Driven Simplification (PDS), which minimizes length approximation error for a given compression target. Both problems are solved within a unified dynamic programming framework, and we provide mathematical proofs establishing that our formulation yields globally optimal solutions. This guarantees flexible, direct control over both compression ratio and length-approximation fidelity. { We benchmark CDS and PDS on real-world AIS datasets spanning diverse navigation scenarios and representative water area, comparing against state-of-the-art baselines. Experimental results on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that even under a small length error tolerance ($\epsilon=0.1$ nmi), our methods achieve about 91\% data compression rate, approximately 14\% higher than the best-performing baseline, which implies that our methods are capable of maximally preserving the trajectory length while reducing data redundancy significant.
item.dc:creator: Enmei Tu, Zhiye Xie, Xixia Xu, Shuhang Chen

item.title: Statistical Elements of a Successful Farm-scale Trial
item.description: arXiv:2610.38297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Growers and advisers increasingly run large strip trials on their own paddocks, but the rules used to design them come from small-plot research. We simulated strip trials on a spatially autocorrelated field, varying trial length (L), replication (r), randomised or systematic allocation, and long-strip or stacked layout, for a nitrogen response that was uniform or varied across within-field pseudo-environments (PEs). Analyses of strip-plot means and of yield pixels were first checked for Type I error, and designs were then compared by the smallest response that a valid analysis detects with 80% power. Follow-up runs added gaps, unequal strip lengths, trends, spatially varying responses and alternative field structures; more than 3 million models were fitted. Treating pixels as independent replicates gave false positives in 32-40% of null trials. Replication was the strongest design lever: the detectable response scaled as $r^{-0.60}$ to $r^{-1.02}$ but only as $L^{-0.45}$ or more slowly, and at equal plot area more, shorter replicates won all 66 comparisons. With complete data, strip means with an autoregressive residual were the most precise analysis; when strips contained gaps, pixel-level spatial models with a strip effect halved the detectable response, while the spatial analysis of strip means became liberal. For PE-varying responses, spatial PE models detected per-PE effects 33-46% smaller than PE means without a spatial term. Randomisation did not improve precision but kept tests valid (systematic allocation: Type I error up to 23%), whereas systematic allocation gave more accurate response maps. The results are condensed into a design table and a detectable-gain chart for use before a trial is sown.
item.dc:creator: Zhanglong Cao, Suman Rakshit, Barbara Kachigunda, Julia Easton, Mark Gibberd

item.title: Compartment-driven Gaussian processes for uncertainty quantification of pharmacokinetic exposures
item.description: arXiv:2610.38325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pharmacokinetic modeling is a crucial part of drug development. An important goal is to estimate patients' total and peak exposure to a drug over time, quantified by the area under the concentration--time curve (AUC) and the maximum concentration ($C_{\max}$) respectively. Such exposure assessment is essential to balance efficacy and safety in medications that offer therapeutic benefits but carry risks of toxicity, such as chemotherapy drugs. Uncertainty quantification for exposure quantities, however, remains challenging, since they are functionals of an often sparsely observed concentration--time curve with measurement errors. We propose a compartment-driven Gaussian process framework that propagates uncertainty in concentration--time curves to pharmacokinetic exposure functionals. Our approach uses pharmacokinetic compartmental models to specify a mechanistically informed prior and Gaussian processes to accommodate departures from the assumed pharmacokinetic dynamics. The framework can accommodate both individual-level and group-aggregated concentration--time data commonly seen in practice. We provide straightforward computational procedures for drawing posterior inference on AUC and $C_{\max}$. Simulations across a range of observation schemes demonstrate robustness to departures from the assumed compartmental dynamics. We apply the method to patient-level datasets on warfarin and theophylline, and aggregated data from a chemotherapy study of 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine in patients with normal or impaired hepatic function. The chemotherapy analysis quantifies drug-specific exposure differences between groups with differing liver function, with potential implications for informing dosing decisions.
item.dc:creator: Sanjay Palta-Hill, Barbara Engelhardt, Edric Tam

item.title: Distributional Flexibility under Box-Cox Normality: A Theoretical and Empirical Evaluation of the Power-Normal Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2610.38454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Methods based on Box-Cox models have recently been developed for inference on clinically interpretable treatment effects in clinical trials. These methods model marginal outcome distributions using the power-normal distribution (PND), but the range of real-world data distributions that it can adequately approximate remains unclear. We evaluated PND approximations using two parameterizations of the four-parameter generalized $F$/generalized beta of the second kind family and 165 laboratory variables from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Overall distributional agreement was assessed using the overlap coefficient and Jensen-Shannon divergence, and location and spread on the original scale were evaluated using relative biases in the median and interquartile range. The PND closely approximated a broad range of smooth unimodal positive distributions in both the theoretical and empirical evaluations. Reduced agreement was associated with pronounced lower-bound accumulation, heaping or discretization, and multicomponent or peak-tail features. These features may be recognizable before fitting and provide practical guidance for assessing the suitability of the PND. We also developed the R package powerNormal for distributional calculations, parameter estimation, reparameterization, and random-number generation for the PND.
item.dc:creator: Kazushi Maruo, Yusuke Yamaguchi, Ryota Ishii, Toshio Shimokawwa, Masahiko Gosho

item.title: Assessing the Role of Green Premium and Localized Price Spillovers in Budget Hotels : Evidence from Delhi National Capital Region (NCR)
item.description: arXiv:2610.38567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sustainable urban tourism depends on how environmental quality, public transport accessibility, and accommo dation clustering shape visitor mobility and destination development. This study examines these relationships in the budget hotel sector of Delhi National Capital Region, India, an emerging mega-destination marked by rapid urban expansion and uneven infrastructure provision. Using data from 857 budget hotels, we estimate a mixed geographically weighted spatial autoregressive model that captures both spatial heterogeneity and localized price spillovers. The model combines hotel attributes with satellite- derived indicators, including vegetation density, built-up area, night-time light intensity, and distances to metro stations, bus stops, airports, city centers, and tourist attractions. Results show that greenery has a place-dependent value: it generates a green premium in dense urban cores, where environmental amenities are scarce, but becomes a discount in peripheral areas where vegetation often reflects weaker tourism infrastructure. Metro accessibility creates a mobility pre mium, highlighting the role of public transport in supporting low-cost tourist movement. Local spatial spillovers reveal agglomeration benefits in established clusters and price cannibalization in peripheral markets. The find ings show how spatially differentiated planning can align green infrastructure, transit investment, and budget accommodation with more sustainable urban tourism development.
item.dc:creator: Shreyash Deshmukh (Indian Institute of Management Kozhikode), Shovan Chowdhury (Indian Institute of Management Kozhikode)

item.title: Challenge or Pass? A Dynamic Policy for MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System
item.description: arXiv:2610.39452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under Major League Baseball's automated ball-strike (ABS) challenge system, players must weigh the value of overturning a call against the risk of losing a challenge they may need later. We develop a policy that values an overturn through its effect on expected runs, accounting for the count, outs, and runners on base. Using pitch tracking and game records, we reconstruct challenge opportunities, including calls that players let stand. A Bayesian model represents players' imperfect impressions of pitch location and uses them to estimate overturn probabilities, with uncertainty calibrated from historical challenge decisions. Dynamic programming compares the expected gain with the future cost of losing a challenge, accounting for the stage of the game, the number of challenges remaining, and opportunities on both offense and defense. We develop the policy using games before the 2026 All-Star break and evaluate it without refitting on 983 games played afterward. Along the recorded sequence of opportunities, the policy recovers 0.536 modeled correction runs per game across both teams, compared with 0.452 under observed decisions, an improvement of 18.5%. The gain is 0.084 runs per game, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.065, 0.103]. The policy makes more challenges and recovers more value per successful review despite a lower overturn rate. These results show why overturn rate alone can be a misleading measure of challenge strategy.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Pipping-Gam\'on, Zach Sissman, Lila Dodson, Abraham J. Wyner

item.title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response
item.description: arXiv:2610.39668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying random spatial variations in composite interface properties is an essential prerequisite for the high-fidelity propagation of material properties variabilities through structural numerical models. This study proposes a multi-scale stochastic framework designed to bridge the gap between local interfacial characterization at the coupon scale and the global response of industrial aerospace panels, focusing specifically on the skin-stringer bond line. Building upon previous stochastic modeling and identification methodologies for Mode I fracture, we first extend the likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II configurations to characterize interfacial stochastic parameters using experimental coupon data. To address the scale-up challenge, we employ a simulation-based Stochastic Finite Element Method (SFEM) to contrast two distinct probabilistic strategies -- spatially uniform variations (Paradigm 2) and spatially correlated random fields (Paradigm 3) -- against the traditional industrial B-basis standard (Paradigm 1). The numerical results reveal a dual mechanism in uncertainty propagation depending on the targeted airframe design criterion. For global performance, such as the ultimate load capacity, a significant scale effect leads to an uncertainty attenuation phenomenon; statistical averaging smooths out local heterogeneities, demonstrating that a computationally efficient spatially uniform approach is sufficient. Conversely, for local integrity, such as the threshold and spatial localization of early damage initiation, the inclusion of spatially correlated random fields becomes indispensable to capture premature degradation driven by local material weak spots. This balanced probabilistic treatment offers a route toward test derisking and predictive uncertainty management in the design of damage-tolerant aerospace composite airframes.
item.dc:creator: Elton Donfack-Siewe, Sylvain Dubreuil, Christian Fagiano, J\'er\^ome Morio, Jean-Philippe Navarro

item.title: A case study of hybrid statistical models for analyzing spatio-temporal effects in historical map series of Donau-Ries county
item.description: arXiv:2610.40513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This case study compares generalized linear models, generalized additive models, and semi-structured deep distributional regression for analyzing settlement patterns in historical land-cover maps. Using four reference years for Donau-Ries county (Landkreis Donau-Ries) in southern Germany, we quantify how distances to agricultural areas, forests, and rivers relate to residential presence, and we evaluate predictive performance through spatial block cross-validation. Classical models yield stable and interpretable distance effects, whereas the semi-structured framework improves prediction once local image context is included. The analysis illustrates a practical trade-off between interpretability, accuracy, and robustness when interpretable covariates are combined with deep components in spatio-temporal data analysis.
item.dc:creator: Mireille Fangueng, Frank Thiemann, Monika Sester, Philipp Otto

item.title: Fast segmentation of watermarked texts from large language models through an epidemic change-point framework
item.description: arXiv:2509.21160v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With the growing use of large language models, concerns over content authenticity have spurred a variety of watermarking schemes. These schemes use secret keys to detect machine-generated text while remaining imperceptible to readers. Detection typically reduces to statistical hypothesis testing for the presence of watermarks, a topic that is now well studied. In contrast, the finer-grained task of localizing which segments of a text are watermarked is much less explored; existing approaches often lack scalability or guarantees robust to paraphrasing and post-editing. We bring a new perspective to this segmentation problem through the lens of epidemic change-points and, by exploiting this connection, propose WISER, a novel and computationally efficient watermark segmentation algorithm. We establish finite-sample error bounds and consistency for detecting multiple watermarked segments in a single text. Complementing these theoretical results, our extensive numerical experiments show that WISER outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods, both in terms of computational speed as well as accuracy, on various benchmark datasets embedded with diverse watermarking schemes. Together, these theoretical and empirical results position WISER as an effective tool for watermark localization and illustrate how classical statistical ideas can yield theoretically valid and computationally efficient solutions to a modern problem of immediate importance.
item.dc:creator: Soham Bonnerjee, Subhrajyoty Roy, Sayar Karmakar

item.title: The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus: harmonising 128 aviation-safety source codes into one deduplicated cross-national accident dataset
item.description: arXiv:2610.37671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: National aviation-investigation databases are deep but territorial; global compilations such as the Aviation Safety Network and the Bureau of Aircraft Accidents Archives are hand-curated, apply their own inclusion thresholds, and publish no per-record lineage. The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus harmonizes 279,485 occurrences and 131,882 attached narratives from 128 source codes -- national accident-investigation authorities, occurrence-reporting systems and four global compilations. Records are mapped into one schema; each normalized record reduces to exactly one key from an ordered ladder -- event signature, registration and date, rounded position and date, or source and native identifier -- so a missing field never creates a link, and the key is the occurrence identifier. Records the ladder cannot reach are scored in a blocked pass into an explicit merge table and applied only within an automatically approved score band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking; one provenance row per contributing source -- its native identifier and URL -- is retained, with attribution and licence terms per source code. Linkage error is measured on five adjudicated samples totalling 200 pairs. A recorded uniform random draw of 60 from the 3,441 merges the automatic band applies as it ships found no error; the exact two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on its false-merge rate is 6.0%, or 205 pairs. The measured error covers the scored band only; the ladder's deterministic joins are not adjudicated. The corpus has no exposure denominators and inherits the under-reporting of its sources. It is offered as a base for cross-national safety statistics, source-disagreement studies and narrative text mining; a frozen, DOI-referenced snapshot accompanies the live API.
item.dc:creator: Denys Kolomiiets

item.title: Weighting Scheme and Construction in IPCW Survival Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.38102v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) is widely used to address dependent censoring in survival analysis. Beyond estimation of the censoring distribution, its implementation requires specifying how inverse probability weights are incorporated into survival estimators. IPCW does not uniquely determine this construction, and different choices can produce different finite-sample behavior even under the same censoring model. In this work, we examine a class of IPCW estimators for the survival function, distinguishing hazard-based from margin-based formulations and time-varying from fixed weighting schemes. We show how these choices affect structural validity, stability, and finite-sample performance. In particular, the weight-changing hazard (WCH) estimator applies time-varying censoring weights within a product-limit construction with risk-set normalization, ensuring monotonicity and boundedness when the weighted risk-set denominators are positive. Through simulation studies under varying levels of covariate-dependent and administrative censoring, we demonstrate that WCH achieves favorable bias--variance tradeoffs and improved finite-sample stability relative to the alternative IPCW constructions examined, particularly in settings with few observed events or heavy censoring. We further illustrate these differences using data from the Women's Interagency HIV Study (WIHS), in which alternative IPCW constructions produced meaningfully different survival curves. Overall, our findings emphasize that the effectiveness of IPCW depends on both the weighting scheme and the estimator formulation. Careful consideration of these choices is therefore important for reliable survival estimation under dependent censoring.
item.dc:creator: Ruohui Chen, Shuhan Liu, Scott Zuo, Lihui Zhao, Hui Zhang, Xin Tu, Dung-Tsa Chen, Qianxing Mo

item.title: FACTS-MAS: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Adaptive Forecasting from Heterogeneous Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.38225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world forecasting often requires integrating heterogeneous evidence whose predictive value varies across horizons, operating regimes, and domains. We introduce FACTS-MAS, a domain-agnostic multi-agent forecasting framework that decomposes evidence into specialized channels for temporal dynamics, exogenous context, seasonality, structural information, and discrete events. Each agent generates an independently testable forecast through a common interface, while leakage-safe historical validation measures its predictive skill relative to a naive reference. These skill estimates are used to weight and combine agent forecasts, so that uninformative evidence is either removed or downweighted rather than forced to participate. A calibration procedure selects domain-specific constant means based on historical validation folds. We evaluate FACTS-MAS on weekly for-sale housing inventory from Zillow and weekly unemployment insurance claims from FRED, for 15 U.S. metropolitan areas at 4-, 8-, and 13-week forecasting horizons. Our method outperforms both a naive last-value forecast method and the TimesFM foundation model. However, a factor-adjusted exponential smoothing model performs as well as the fused forecast. The evidence therefore supports FACTS-MAS as a systematic protocol for testing, calibrating, and recomposing evidence channels before assembling them into the strongest single model for a specific application domain. Code, data, and results are available at https://github.com/Madumita24/FACTS-MAS.
item.dc:creator: Madumita Karthikeyan, Umang Rajnikant Bid, Rong Pan

item.title: Combining Adaptive Seamless Phase II/III Designs and Group Sequential Analysis for Time-to-Event Endpoints in Oncology Trials
item.description: arXiv:2610.38301v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Seamless Phase II/III designs are a natural vehicle for the randomized dose optimization called for by the US Food and Drug Administration's Project Optimus initiative. Their extension to group sequential repeated testing of a time-to-event endpoint after end-of-Phase-II dose selection, however, remains largely unestablished. Existing proposals index the boundaries for the post-selection looks by the overall information fraction of the primary endpoint---the correct index for the log-rank statistics of an unadapted trial, but not for the combination statistics these designs actually test---and support family-wise error rate (FWER) control by simulation. We instead work from the joint distribution of the combination statistics themselves, calibrating group sequential boundaries separately for each hypothesis in the closure and applying closed testing at every look; a general lemma establishes that this controls the FWER in the strong sense, for any number of hypotheses and analysis times. Specifically, under patient-wise separation and an inverse-normal combination test, the interim and final statistics for an individual hypothesis are bivariate normal, with a correlation determined by how the events at each look divide between the pre- and post-selection cohorts rather than by the overall information fraction, so that their boundaries follow from standard group sequential software; the corresponding statistics for the intersection hypothesis, formed from a Hochberg-adjusted Stage-1 $p$-value, are not multivariate normal, and we obtain their boundaries by a dedicated numerical integration. Head-to-head against a recently proposed incremental-Dunnett procedure, the two were near-identical when the design projections were correct, but ours was more robust when the combination weights were based on a misprojected division of the Stage~1 events either side of the interim.
item.dc:creator: Wentian Guo, Qingyu Chen, Chi Song, Jiabu Ye, Chintu Desai, Victor Zhang, Rui Miao

item.title: The Hidden Value of Soft Infrastructure for Urban Flood Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2610.38896v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As sea level rises and flooding events become more frequent, cities are tapping into a range of engineering and planning solutions to reduce flood losses. Beyond traditional ``hard'' infrastructure (e.g., sewage, seawalls), ``soft'' infrastructure that supports and empowers the role of citizens in preparedness has been hailed as a promising avenue for improving adaptation. Despite its promise, there have been very limited attempts to quantify its effectiveness in reducing losses relative to hard infrastructure, particularly in urban environments. This study fills this knowledge gap using generative AI to quantify the effectiveness of a range of hard and soft infrastructure in urban areas. We demonstrate, for the first time, that soft infrastructure can significantly reduce flood losses, with an impact on par with hard infrastructure. Our results open the door to novel ways of confronting adaptation challenges in cities. Soft infrastructure is a viable alternative, especially when budgetary or time constraints make hard infrastructure unattainable. Policymakers should also couple soft and hard infrastructure to maximize resilience.
item.dc:creator: Lidia Cano Pecharroman, ChangHoon Hahn

item.title: Modular Bayesian Foundation Models: Bayesian time series encoders for OOD detection, routing and forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.39043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Industrial systems continuously generate time series that vary in sampling frequency, scale, dynamics, and operating regime. Consequently a single time-series foundation model may not be able to represent all regimes effectively and retraining a large model for every new dataset or regime shift is computationally expensive. Modular foundation models address this issue by reusing specialised encoders trained on diverse datasets and by allowing the expansion of capabilities through the addition of new experts. This approach requires compact experts to minimize storage cost and a proper selection mechanism of experts for unseen data. We propose a modular foundation model framework that combines end-to-end Bayesian encoder training with uncertainty based routing. Using Singular Bayesian Neural Networks (SBNNs), we build a collection of compact Bayesian encoders whose epistemic uncertainty guides label-free selection. At the selected ranks, our Bayesian collection uses 63.8\% less storage than its deterministic counterpart. We evaluate this framework on time-series data through distribution shift, encoder selection, and probabilistic forecasting. Across seven incoming datasets, uncertainty-based routing is competitive with distance-based routing in terms of forecast MSE, while reducing average ECE from 0.086 to 0.072 and average NLL from 0.907 to 0.836. It also increases PICP90 from 82.28\% to 89.03\%. In a separate model-family comparison, we evaluate the SBNN pipeline against full-rank Bayes by Backprop, deep ensembles, and MC Dropout. The SBNN pipeline achieves an average MSE of 0.390, comparable with 0.396 for deep ensembles, 0.389 for MC dropout, and 0.443 for the full-rank Bayesian model. It uses 63.9\% fewer parameters than MC dropout, 81.9\% fewer than the full-rank model, and 92.8\% fewer than the deep ensemble.
item.dc:creator: Mame Diarra Toure, Quang Hung Pham, Mohamed Ryad Zemouri, David Stephens, Luc Vouligny, Martin Gagnon

item.title: TwinPoSI: Statistical Twins for Powerful Post-Selection Inference on Population-Based Regression Coefficients
item.description: arXiv:2610.39274v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-selection inference (PoSI) quantifies uncertainty about regression coefficients after data-driven feature selection. A central question is the inferential target. Projection-based targets are the coefficients of the best linear approximation restricted to the selected features and depend on the selection procedure, whereas population-based targets are the selected features' coefficients in the full linear model and are often more relevant for scientific interpretation. The two targets can differ, even in sign. Existing PoSI methods largely focus on projection-based targets and may yield overly wide confidence intervals. We propose TwinPoSI (statistical twin post-selection inference), a method for powerful PoSI on population-based targets with false coverage rate (FCR) control. TwinPoSI leverages \textit{statistical twins}, defined as synthetic datasets generated from a fitted model to mimic the original data. With generating parameters known, statistical twins enable direct calibration of confidence intervals for bias introduced by data-dependent feature selection. We establish that TwinPoSI controls the FCR at the nominal level, up to Monte Carlo error and an asymptotically negligible approximation error. Moreover, in a Gaussian linear model with an orthogonal design, TwinPoSI uniquely attains the oracle average interval length to first order among the methods considered. Simulations show that TwinPoSI maintains reliable FCR control for both population-based and projection-based targets while yielding shorter confidence intervals and higher power than the competing methods. In riboflavin production data, TwinPoSI identifies associated genes, quantifies their directions and magnitudes of association, and yields the shortest average intervals among the methods considered.
item.dc:creator: Changhu Wang, Zhifei Li, Jingyi Jessica Li

item.title: Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert Review: Application to Online Cell-Type Labeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.40252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models can accelerate cell-type annotation in digital pathology, but safely scaling their use requires determining, with error control, which model-generated labels can be accepted without expert review. This is challenging in evolving workflows because cell morphology and type composition may change across tissue regions and slides, making one-time calibration unreliable. We propose Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert review under Distribution shift (CARED), a distribution-free framework that leverages randomized expert audit to achieve long-run error control for AI-assisted annotation under distribution shift. For each incoming batch, CARED uniformly selects a subset of cases for expert review and uses the acquired labels to calibrate later decisions. Among unreviewed cases, CARED determines a subset of them to safely skip expert labeling, while suggesting candidate labels for the others for downstream resolution. We prove that this workflow provides long-run control of cumulative error over both the full stream and the cells outside of the audit sample, without stationarity or exchangeability assumptions. We further enhance the framework by introducing class-conditional guarantees to ensure error control within important but rare cell types, together with a utility module to target more automatic resolutions, smaller candidate sets, and greater biological coherence, without compromising validity. Experiments on pancreas, lung, and ovary annotation streams, together with a stream constructed from real expert annotations, show that CARED controls the cumulative errors while a substantial fraction of cells (up to 70%) bypass expert review.
item.dc:creator: Xuhe Zhang, Zhi Huang, Ying Jin

item.title: Real-time Win Probability and Latent Player Ability via STATS X in Team Sports
item.description: arXiv:2602.19513v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study proposes a statistically grounded framework for real-time win probability evaluation and player assessment in score-based team sports, based on minute-by-minute cumulative box-score data. We introduce a continuous dominance indicator (T-score) that maps final scores to real values consistent with win/lose outcomes, and formulate it as a time-evolving stochastic representation (T-process) driven by standardized cumulative statistics. This structure captures temporal game dynamics and enables sequential, analytically tractable updates of in-game win probability. Through this stochastic formulation, competitive advantage is decomposed into interpretable statistical components. Furthermore, we define a latent contribution index, STATS X, which quantifies a player's involvement in favorable dominance intervals identified by the T-process. This allows us to separate a team's baseline strength from game-specific performance fluctuations and provides a coherent, structural evaluation framework for both teams and players. While we do not implement AI methods in this paper, our framework is positioned as a foundational step toward hybrid integration with AI. By providing a structured time-series representation of dominance with an explicit probabilistic interpretation, the framework enables flexible learning mechanisms and incorporation of high-dimensional data, while preserving statistical coherence and interpretability. This work provides a basis for advancing AI-driven sports analytics.
item.dc:creator: Yasutaka Shimizu, Atsushi Yamanobe

item.title: Critique of "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses ..." by John O' Quigley
item.description: arXiv:2606.29394v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The paper "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses suspected of inflicting deliberate harm on patients" by Prof. John O'Quigley explores an interesting hypothesis concerning statistical information hidden in the part of the infamous Lucy Letby roster chart pertaining to the 37 other nurses. Unfortunately, we have to point out some serious errors in his statistical analyses. The data actually contains information which strongly disproves his main modelling assumption. We do, however, strongly agree with him that from a forensic statistical point of view, the roster chart is fake evidence which should not have been shown to jurors.
item.dc:creator: Richard D. Gill

item.title: Adaptive Inference in Multivariate Nonparametric Regression Models Under Monotonicity
item.description: arXiv:2011.14219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider the problem of adaptive inference on a regression function at a point under a multivariate nonparametric regression setting. The regression function belongs to a H\"older class and is assumed to be monotone with respect to some or all of the arguments. We derive the minimax rate of convergence for confidence intervals (CIs) that adapt to the underlying smoothness, and provide an adaptive inference procedure that obtains this minimax rate. When the regression function is monotone in $k_{+}$ of its $k$ arguments, the minimax expected length over a H\"older class with exponent $\gamma'$ of CIs that maintain coverage over a rougher class with exponent $\gamma$ is of order $n^{-1/(2+k_{+}/\gamma'+(k-k_{+})/\gamma)}$. The rate is unchanged if the rougher class restricts the smoothness only at the point, along the nonmonotone arguments. Under monotonicity along a closed convex cone that contains no line, only the dimension of its linear span enters the rate. The procedure differs from that of Cai and Low (2004), intended to yield shorter CIs under practically relevant specifications. It is valid in finite samples under Gaussian errors with a known variance. The proposed method applies to general linear functionals of the regression function.
item.dc:creator: Koohyun Kwon, Soonwoo Kwon

item.title: Subgroup comparisons within and across studies in meta-analysis
item.description: arXiv:2508.15531v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Meta-analyses of published subgroup-level data may yield different interaction estimates depending on how the available data are weighted across studies. In particular, the difference between meta-analytic subgroup-specific effects need not equal the meta-analysis of within-study subgroup differences when these quantities are based on different study weights. Variation in subgroup prevalence across trials, including the presence of single-subgroup trials, may further amplify this discrepancy and introduce aggregation bias into across-study subgroup comparisons. We examine established approaches for jointly or separately estimating subgroup-specific effects and treatment-by-subgroup interactions and introduce the Same Weighting Across Different Analyses (SWADA) principle. SWADA applies a common set of study weights across the connected subgroup and interaction analyses, thereby guaranteeing algebraic agreement between the difference of subgroup averages and the average subgroup difference. Through simulation studies and meta-analyses of randomised trials of COVID-19 treatments, we compare several SWADA weighting schemes with existing approaches in terms of bias, coverage, precision, and root mean squared error. SWADA ensures internally coherent subgroup and interaction estimates, but may require down-weighting or excluding studies that provide information for only one subgroup. The choice of weights therefore involves a trade- off between algebraic coherence, use of the available subgroup evidence, and statistical efficiency. SWADA should be viewed as a general weighting principle for meta-analytic comparisons rather than as a universally preferable estimator.
item.dc:creator: Renato Panaro, Christian R\"over, Tim Friede

item.title: Consistent Bayesian meta-analysis on subgroup specific effects and interactions
item.description: arXiv:2512.18785v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clinical trials commonly report effects on the full study population as well as for patient subgroups. Random-effects meta-analyses of subgroup-specific effects and treatment-by-subgroup interactions might be misaligned, especially when subgroups contribute differently to study populations. We show that, after contribution adjustment, subgroup meta-analysis can recover the same interaction inference regardless of whether interaction or subgroup data are used. Our framework for subgroup-data interaction meta-analysis has four advantages. First, it adjusts for variation in relative subgroup contribution, quantified by the within-trial information fraction. Second, it is robust to prevalence imbalance and variation. Third, it provides a self-contained model-based approach. Fourth, it can incorporate prior information into Bayesian interaction meta-analysis. The method demonstration uses an example application including 7 trials of disease-modifying therapies in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; the contribution-adjusted model manages to reproduce the results from the interaction meta-analysis while yielding matching estimates for the subgroup effects. By controlling subgroup contribution while retaining subgroup interpretability, this approach allows for interaction decision-making when published subgroup data are available. Although the proposed model is presented in the Bayesian context, it can also be implemented in frequentist or likelihood frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Renato Panaro, Christian R\"over, Tim Friede

item.title: Semiparametric Inference for Functional Difference-in-Differences
item.description: arXiv:2605.26964v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the functional average treatment effect on the treated in a two-period difference-in-differences design. Under conditional functional parallel trends, we derive the full-curve efficient influence function and efficiency bound and construct a cross-fitted, doubly robust estimator. Under ultra-dense observation, bounds on curve-estimation error and learner stability preserve its full-data first-order behavior. Nuisance-rate and moment conditions yield asymptotic linearity in $L^2$; additional Sobolev regularity gives uniform Gaussian limits and valid continuous-domain bands computed on a refining grid. In simulations, estimation errors decrease with sample size under single-model misspecification, and bands accounting for nuisance estimation have near-nominal or conservative coverage. Further experiments examine basis-truncation bias and nuisance-estimation uncertainty. An application to electricity load profiles from 4389 eligible households estimates a modest reduction concentrated in evening consumption among dynamic-tariff participants.
item.dc:creator: Junzhu Nie, Chengxiu Ling, Mengfei Ran

item.title: The Model as One Rater Among Several: Measuring Political Positions in Data-Sparse Regions with a Language-Model Panel
item.description: arXiv:2606.23042v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most instruments for measuring political positions, such as manifesto coding, expert surveys and text-scaling models, were built and validated on Western party systems, and they break down worst where many consequential actors never publish a manifesto, never contest a competitive election, or commit one position to a charter and act on another in office. This paper proposes a method for such settings. I treat a large language model as a single fallible rater in a panel, the way an expert survey treats one expert, and describe the panel, its synthesis, an applicability rule that keeps a blank distinct from a zero, and a lens that separates what an actor declares from what it does. Three results follow. First, a built-in experiment isolates the rubric: with a definition-free round held fixed, written axis definitions move scores by a mean of 1.8 points on a 21-point scale and tighten agreement between raters (mean absolute gap 2.81 to 2.50; r 0.81 to 0.89). Second, across nine models from eight laboratories in two countries, Krippendorff's alpha is 0.86 on an interval and 0.87 on an ordinal metric, and it held as the panel grew from five raters to nine. This is reliability and says nothing yet about validity, since models trained on overlapping data can share a bias no statistic computed from the models can detect. Third, the panel's sharpest split, a bimodal divergence on an actor's stance toward the state's foundational order, comes from a referent problem: the models agree on the facts and differ on which order counts as the regime. A blind triple-coding traces about two-thirds of such disagreement to interpretation. The worked example is the Middle East and North Africa, and the rubric, prompt and data are released in full.
item.dc:creator: Tarek Gara

item.title: The Dirichlet Process as sampling distribution
item.description: arXiv:2607.26185v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Dirichlet process (DP) is the most common Bayesian nonparametric prior, however, its properties as sampling distribution have not been studied nor inference on its parameters. Here we use the DP as a data generating model and make Bayesian inference on its centering measure and precision parameter. We illustrate with a sequence of histograms as observed data. In particular, we consider simulated and real datasets.
item.dc:creator: Luis E. Nieto-Barajas

item.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2609.07033v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Estimating an instrumental variables (IV) first stage with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary and penalty. Existing rules target first-stage objectives, although these choices affect structural estimation. We derive a feasible approximate mean squared error (AMSE) criterion for full-sample IV-LASSO with one endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors. For a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty pairs, the criterion trades off approximation of the optimal instrument against a complexity cost that depends on the first two moments of the LASSO effective dimension and on the degree of endogeneity. The selected pair attains the smallest candidate-specific AMSE component up to vanishing relative error. In simulations calibrated to Paravisini et al. (2015), the criterion improves substantially on the plug-in rule at low endogeneity and on cross-validation at high endogeneity, with nearly identical results under non-Gaussian errors. A supplementary appendix formally extends analysis to a class of non-Gaussian errors.
item.dc:creator: Yukun Ma, Manu Navjeevan, Bogdan Salahub

item.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.19098v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.
item.dc:creator: Simon Hellmann, Leander Lerch, Terrance Wilms, Moritz Reumsch\"ussel, Alberto Meola, F\'elix Delory, Steffi Knorn, Stefan Streif, S\"oren Weinrich
